correctness.rationale: Translation retains the frequency set and uniform convergence. On [-pi,pi], the normalized moments against 1 and cos(t) are a sin(pi alpha)/(pi alpha) and a alpha sin(pi alpha)/(pi(1-alpha^2)); the integer modes n>=2 and all sine terms make no contribution. A continuous nonnegative nonzero restriction has strictly positive integral against 1-cos(t), so its first cosine moment must be strictly less than its mean. The computed ratio is at least one precisely on the asserted oscillatory side, including the endpoint. If the whole restriction is zero, the mean forces a=0 and the sin(t) moment has nonzero coefficient sin(pi alpha)/(pi(1-alpha^2)) for b; the remaining integer coefficients then vanish by orthogonality. Applying the same argument to -f yields both signs. Below the threshold, the normalized displaced cosine has mean one and nth cosine coefficient 2(-1)^n alpha^2/(alpha^2-n^2). Subtracting it from the Poisson kernel with r=alpha^2/(1-alpha^2) removes exactly the constant and first harmonic; the continuous periodic difference has absolutely summable coefficients and hence equals its Fourier series, including at the matching endpoints. Poisson positivity follows from 0<r<1. Continuity also gives strict signs in the open window whenever both signs occur on its closure. The proof uses the stated uniform convergence and covers irrational as well as rational alpha.
residual_risks: Numerical comparisons in the supplied checker are supplementary; the strict critical conclusion follows from the integral, not floating-point comparisons.

value.rationale: A one-mode perturbation at the integer period is the natural minimal test of general small-perturbation sign-oscillation theorems. The exact threshold separates oscillation from strict positivity, closes the borderline case, and shows how far a general sufficient bound can be improved in a canonical slice. The explicit witness and dual obstruction have complementary uses when studying further missing modes or observation lengths.
